docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The public API follows one pipeline:

load data → list trials → plot → save

import scanpath_studio as sps

words, fixations = sps.load_scanpath_data("ia.csv", "fixations.csv")
fig = sps.plot_scanpath(words, fixations, participant="p1", trial="t3")
sps.save_figure(fig, "scanpath.html")

Every function on this page is importable from scanpath_studio. The figure builders also take any of the figure options as a keyword.

docs.title: Column names
docs.text:
Columns keep the names your files give them. The demo's word table calls its word id IA_ID and its total fixation duration IA_DWELL_TIME, and every function and option takes those names. A column Scanpath Studio made keeps its internal name. load_scanpath_data(..., names="canonical") gives the internal names, which are the same for every dataset. On the bundled demo, the first steps print this (run when the docs are built):

import scanpath_studio as sps

words, fixations = sps.load_sample_data()
print(sps.list_trials(words, fixations).head(3))

columns = ["IA_ID", "IA_LABEL", "IA_FIRST_FIXATION_DURATION", "IA_DWELL_TIME"]
print(words[columns].head(3))

1       l37_1129  l37_1129_2_1_2_Ele_r0
2       l37_1129  l37_1129_2_1_3_Adv_r0

docs.title: load_scanpath_data
docs.text:
load_scanpath_data(
    words=None,
    fixations=None,
    *,
    word_schema=None,
    fix_schema=None,
    trial_parts_manifest=None,
    image_root=None,
    image_pattern=DEFAULT_STIMULUS_IMAGE_PATTERN,
    keep_columns=None,
    names=NAMES_SOURCE,
)

Load and normalize a words table and/or a fixations table.

Columns keep the names your files give them: CURRENT_FIX_DURATION, not duration_ms. A column Scanpath Studio built, converted, computed or changed keeps its internal name, and data.column_names records what every column was called. Every API function takes these frames, and every column option (color_by=, the hover fields …) takes either name.

Columns are auto-detected from EyeLink, Gazepoint, Tobii, SMI, Pupil Labs and snake_case names. Normalization keeps the mapped fields and the recognized optional ones (eye, EyeLink's interest-area measures, linguistic features …) and drops the rest, unless keep_columns names them.

  • One table is enough. Leave out the table a dataset doesn't have: it comes back as an empty frame, and the plots skip that layer.
  • Stimulus-level words. A words table without a participant column holds each text's word boxes once, and they are copied onto every trial in the fixations. Each trial is matched by its trial id, else the trial id it had before a repeat's _r2 suffix, else its text_id (for trial ids that embed the participant). Trials that match none raise a data.StimulusJoinWarning (a UserWarning).
  • Fixations without x/y but with a word or AOI id are placed at the centers of their word boxes.
  • Bookkeeping columns. Columns named in data.INTERNAL_COLUMNS are the pipeline's own; data.drop_internal_columns removes them.

Parameters:

  • words (TablesLike | None, default: None ) –

    The words (AOI) table: a DataFrame; a .csv, .tsv, .txt, .tab, .parquet, .feather, .xlsx or .xls file, or a .zip of them; a glob pattern; or a list of paths. Several files (one per participant and/or text) are concatenated, with each file's stem in a source_file column.

  • fixations (TablesLike | None, default: None ) –

    The fixations table, in any form words takes.

  • word_schema (dict | None, default: None ) –

    A mapping from field to column name for the words table, replacing auto-detection. Start from propose_schema.

  • fix_schema (dict | None, default: None ) –

    The same for the fixations table.

  • trial_parts_manifest (dict | None, default: None ) –

    A nested parent-trial/parts definition, for datasets whose tables identify screens through arbitrary selector columns. Explicit screen_id / screen_index columns can instead be mapped in each schema.

  • image_root (str | Path | None, default: None ) –

    A local folder of stimulus images, one page per trial (or screen). Each row the pattern finds a file for gets it as its image_path; a row without one keeps the image_path it had. show_stimulus_image=True then draws the page under the figure. attach_stimulus_images does the same for frames already loaded.

  • image_pattern (str, default: DEFAULT_STIMULUS_IMAGE_PATTERN ) –

    The file to look for under image_root, with {placeholders} naming the rows' canonical columns: "{text_id}.png", "{participant_id}/{trial_id}.png".

  • keep_columns (Iterable[str] | None, default: None ) –

    Further columns of your own to carry through under their own names, such as a pupil size or a detection confidence, from whichever table has them, so a figure can color, hover or plot by them. The app's Extra fields to keep; render --keep-columns.

  • names (str, default: NAMES_SOURCE ) –

    "source" keeps the dataset's column names; "canonical" returns the internal names, the same for every dataset, for code that works across datasets.

Returns:

  • ScanpathData –

    The normalized (words, fixations) frames, as a ScanpathData.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    A required field can't be found. The message names the field, the column names auto-detection looked for, and the columns the table has.

  • ValueError –

    image_root does not exist, or image_pattern is absolute or climbs out of it.

  • StimulusJoinError –

    A stimulus-level words table shares neither a trial id nor a text_id with any trial (or, multipart, with every screen a trial has fixations on). A ValueError.

  • UnplacedFixationsError –

    The fixations map no x/y and their word/AOI id column holds no numbers, so none could be placed. A ValueError.

docs.title: ScanpathData
docs.text:
Bases: tuple

The (words, fixations) frames load_scanpath_data returns, with their names.

It is a tuple, so words, fixations = load_scanpath_data(…) unpacks it, and .words / .fixations name the two frames. column_names holds the dataset's own name for every canonical column, per table: {"words": ColumnNames, "fixations": ColumnNames}.

With names="source" (the default) the frames' columns are the dataset's own names and each frame carries its map, so any API function takes it, sliced, filtered or merged, and the names it writes are yours. With names="canonical" they are the internal names, the same for every dataset.

docs.title: propose_schema
docs.text:
propose_schema(table, kind='words')

Find the column mapping auto-detection would use for a raw table.

It is the mapping load_scanpath_data infers, so it is the place to start when detection got a field wrong or could not find one: edit the dict and pass it back as word_schema= or fix_schema=.

Parameters:

  • table (TablesLike) –

    A raw, not yet normalized table: a DataFrame, a path, a glob or a list of paths, as the loader takes.

  • kind (str, default: 'words' ) –

    "words", "fixations" or "raw_gaze".

Returns:

  • dict –

    {canonical field: source column}, with None for a field it could not find.

Examples:

schema = sps.propose_schema("ia.csv", "words")
schema["trial"] = "TRIAL_LABEL"
words, fixations = sps.load_scanpath_data(
    "ia.csv", "fix.csv", word_schema=schema
)

docs.title: attach_stimulus_images
docs.text:
attach_stimulus_images(
    words,
    fixations,
    image_root,
    image_pattern=DEFAULT_STIMULUS_IMAGE_PATTERN,
)

Fill image_path from a folder of stimulus images, on frames already loaded.

It is load_scanpath_data's image_root / image_pattern, for frames that came from somewhere else, such as a corpus loader, which takes no folder. The rules are the same: the placeholders name the rows' canonical columns, and a row the pattern finds no file for keeps the image_path it had.

Parameters:

  • words (DataFrame | None) –

    The words frame, or None.

  • fixations (DataFrame | None) –

    The fixations frame, or None.

  • image_root (str | Path) –

    The folder of stimulus images.

  • image_pattern (str, default: DEFAULT_STIMULUS_IMAGE_PATTERN ) –

    The file to look for under image_root, as in load_scanpath_data.

Returns:

  • ScanpathData –

    New (words, fixations) frames, under the names they came in. The frames passed in are not modified.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    image_root does not exist, or image_pattern is absolute or climbs out of it.

Examples:

words, fixations = sps.attach_stimulus_images(
    *sps.load_potec("data/PoTeC", readers=[0], texts=["b0"]),
    "pages/",
    "{text_id}.png",
)
sps.plot_scanpath(words, fixations, show_stimulus_image=True)

docs.title: load_raw_gaze
docs.text:
load_raw_gaze(table, *, raw_gaze_schema=None, names=NAMES_SOURCE)

Load and normalize a raw, sample-level gaze table, for raw_gaze=.

Raw gaze is the third table plot_scanpath can draw, under the fixations: one row per eye-tracker sample, with a participant, a trial, x / y and usually a timestamp. plot_scanpath keeps only the plotted trial's (and screen's) samples, so one table can serve a whole corpus.

Parameters:

  • table (TablesLike) –

    A DataFrame, path, glob or list of paths, as load_scanpath_data takes. Columns are auto-detected the same way.

  • raw_gaze_schema (dict | None, default: None ) –

    A mapping from field to column, replacing auto-detection. Start from propose_schema(table, "raw_gaze").

  • names (str, default: NAMES_SOURCE ) –

    "source" keeps the table's column names; "canonical" returns the internal ones.

Returns:

  • DataFrame –

    The normalized samples.

Examples:

raw_gaze = sps.load_raw_gaze("gaze_samples.csv")
fig = sps.plot_scanpath(words, fixations, "p1", "t3", raw_gaze=raw_gaze)

docs.title: load_participant_metadata
docs.text:
load_participant_metadata(table, *, id_column=None, participants=None)

Load a participant-level metadata table: one row per participant.

Nothing is broadcast onto the words or fixations frames. Use scanpath_studio.metadata.project to attach chosen columns to a per-trial frame, or .values_for(pid) for one participant.

Parameters:

  • table (TablesLike) –

    A DataFrame, or a path or glob to a CSV, TSV, Parquet or Excel file, or a list of them, stacked into one table. It holds an id column plus anything known about each participant (native_language, age, a comprehension score).

  • id_column (str | None, default: None ) –

    The participant-id column. Defaults to the first recognized spelling (participant_id, subject, RECORDING_SESSION_LABEL, …).

  • participants (DataFrame | list | None, default: None ) –

    A normalized frame or a list of ids to validate the join against. The result's .report then names the participants missing from either side.

Returns:

  • ParticipantMetadata –

    A ParticipantMetadata: the cleaned frame, a field registry (name, label, grain, dtype, missingness) and the join report.

Examples:

words, fixations = sps.load_sample_data()
meta = sps.load_participant_metadata("readers.csv", participants=fixations)
meta.names  # ('native_language', 'age')

docs.title: load_trial_metadata
docs.text:
load_trial_metadata(
    table, *, id_column=None, participant_column=None, trials=None
)

Load a trial-level metadata table: one row per trial.

The sibling of load_participant_metadata, one grain down. Nothing is broadcast onto the words or fixations frames.

The key is yours to state, and it changes what the table means. Keyed by trial id alone, a row describes a text, and every trial of it inherits that row. Keyed by participant and trial (participant_column), a row describes one trial. Nothing in a file says which a corpus is, so this is never inferred.

Parameters:

  • table (TablesLike) –

    A DataFrame or file(s), as load_participant_metadata takes, stacked into one table. It holds a trial-id column plus anything known about each trial (a list name, a condition, a per-trial comprehension score).

  • id_column (str | None, default: None ) –

    The trial-id column. Defaults to the first recognized spelling (trial_id, item_id, TRIAL_INDEX, …).

  • participant_column (str | None, default: None ) –

    The participant-id column, to key each row by participant and trial. Left out, rows are keyed by trial id alone.

  • trials (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    A normalized fixations or words frame, or any frame with participant_id and trial_id, to validate the join against. The result's .report then names the trials missing from either side.

Returns:

  • TrialMetadata –

    A TrialMetadata: the cleaned frame, a field registry and the join report.

Examples:

words, fixations = sps.load_sample_data()
meta = sps.load_trial_metadata("readings.csv", trials=fixations)
meta.names  # ('list_name', 'comprehension_score')

docs.title: load_text_metadata
docs.text:
load_text_metadata(table, *, id_column=None, texts=None)

Load a text-level metadata table: one row per text.

A text is a stimulus, not something one participant owns, so the table is never keyed by participant. Nothing is broadcast onto the words or fixations frames.

Parameters:

  • table (TablesLike) –

    A DataFrame or file(s), as load_participant_metadata takes, stacked into one table. It holds a text-id column plus anything known about each text (genre, difficulty, a stimulus-level comprehension score).

  • id_column (str | list[str] | None, default: None ) –

    The text-id column, or several columns that build a composite id, as the data's own Text ID mapping can. Defaults to the first recognized spelling (text_id, paragraph_id, stimulus_id, …).

  • texts (DataFrame | list | None, default: None ) –

    A normalized fixations or words frame, or any iterable of text ids, to validate the join against. The result's .report then names the texts missing from either side.

Returns:

  • TextMetadata –

    A TextMetadata: the cleaned frame, a field registry and the join report.

Examples:

words, fixations = sps.load_sample_data()
meta = sps.load_text_metadata("texts.csv", texts=words)
meta.names  # ('genre', 'difficulty')

docs.title: load_potec
docs.text:
load_potec(
    root, *, readers=None, texts=None, download=False, names="source"
)

Load PoTeC as normalized (words, fixations) frames, ready to plot.

A participant is a PoTeC reader id, as a string. A trial is one reader's reading of one text, <reader>_<text> ("0_b0"), and its text_id is the text: b0–b5 are biology, p0–p5 physics. The full corpus is 75 readers × 12 texts = 900 trials.

PoTeC's monitor was 1680×1050 (DELL P2210, 60 Hz). Pass that as canvas_size to plot_scanpath for true-to-scale rendering.

Parameters:

  • root (str | Path) –

    A clone of the PoTeC repository with its eye-tracking data downloaded, or any folder to download into.

  • readers (Iterable | None, default: None ) –

    Load only these readers ([0, 1]).

  • texts (Iterable[str] | None, default: None ) –

    Load only these texts (["b0", "p3"]).

  • download (bool, default: False ) –

    Fetch the files the load needs into root on first use, about 10 MB.

  • names (str, default: 'source' ) –

    "source" for PoTeC's own column names, "canonical" for the internal ones (see api.load_scanpath_data).

Returns:

  • tuple[DataFrame, DataFrame] –

    The normalized (words, fixations) frames.

Examples:

import scanpath_studio as sps

words, fixations = sps.load_potec("data/PoTeC", readers=[0], texts=["b0"])
fig = sps.plot_scanpath(words, fixations, "0", "0_b0", canvas_size=(1680, 1050))

docs.title: load_onestop
docs.text:
load_onestop(
    root,
    *,
    regime="ordinary",
    parts=None,
    variant="public",
    download=False,
    names="source",
)

Load OneStop as normalized (words, fixations) frames, ready to plot.

OneStop's presentation monitor was 2560×1440 px (Dell U2715H; Berzak et al. 2025, Methods → Apparatus). Pass that as canvas_size to plot_scanpath for true-to-scale rendering. The reports already match the bundled demo's schema, so they load through the same auto-detection as any other data.

Parameters:

  • root (str | Path) –

    A folder holding the OneStop reports, or (public variant only) to download them into.

  • regime (str, default: 'ordinary' ) –

    "ordinary", "information_seeking", "repeated" or "information_seeking_repeated".

  • parts (Iterable[str] | None, default: None ) –

    Any subset of Title, Question_Preview, Paragraph, Questions, Answers, QA and Feedback. Left out, Paragraph.

  • variant (str, default: 'public' ) –

    "public" for the OSF release, "lacclab" for the lab's local export.

  • download (bool, default: False ) –

    Fetch the chosen regime and parts into root on first use. The public reports are large.

  • names (str, default: 'source' ) –

    "source" for OneStop's own column names, "canonical" for the internal ones (see api.load_scanpath_data).

Returns:

  • tuple[DataFrame, DataFrame] –

    The normalized (words, fixations) frames.

Examples:

import scanpath_studio as sps

words, fixations = sps.load_onestop(
    "data/OneStop", regime="ordinary", parts=["Paragraph"], download=True
)
pid, tid = sps.list_trials(words, fixations).iloc[0]  # one reading
fig = sps.plot_scanpath(words, fixations, pid, tid, canvas_size=(2560, 1440))

docs.title: list_trials
docs.text:
list_trials(words=None, fixations=None, *, raw_gaze=None)

List every plottable trial: one row per participant and trial.

Every trial any table has, whether the words, the fixations or the raw gaze, appears once. The app's trial picker, render --list-trials and the export bundle list the same set. A trial a table lacks plots without that layer: one with words but no fixations draws its text alone, one with fixations but no words its scanpath over no word boxes.

Parameters:

  • words (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    The words frame, or None when the dataset has none.

  • fixations (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    The fixations frame, or None. Pass None for both for a dataset recorded as raw gaze alone.

  • raw_gaze (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    A frame from load_raw_gaze.

Returns:

  • DataFrame –

    The participant and trial ids, sorted by participant, then trial, under the names the frames carry.

docs.text:
list_parts(
    words, fixations, participant=None, trial=None, *, raw_gaze=None
)

List the ordered screens of multipart data, optionally for one trial.

A trial recorded as raw gaze alone takes its screens from raw_gaze (its screen_id). That is decided per trial, so a samples-only trial keeps its screens in a dataset whose other trials have fixations.

Parameters:

  • words (DataFrame | None) –

    The words frame, or None.

  • fixations (DataFrame | None) –

    The fixations frame, or None.

  • participant (str | None, default: None ) –

    Narrow to this participant's trials.

  • trial (str | None, default: None ) –

    Narrow to this trial.

  • raw_gaze (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    A frame from load_raw_gaze.

Returns:

  • DataFrame –

    One row per screen, in order; an empty table for single-screen data.

check_data_health(words=None, fixations=None, raw_gaze=None)

Find values that loaded as numbers but cannot be right: the app's Data checks.

The checks look for fixations lasting 0 ms or less or with an infinite duration or onset, fixations and raw-gaze samples whose position is missing or infinite, word boxes with no area or no finite position, and per-screen screen sizes that are not finite and positive. Nothing is changed or dropped.

Each row of the result is one check that found something:

Column What it holds table, check, problem Where it looked, and what it found columns The columns it read, in the names the frames carry rows, of_rows How many rows, of how many trials The trials those rows fall in breakdown The rows by kind severity "note" for raw-gaze gaps, which blinks and track loss make ordinary what_happens What the app does with those rows examples A few of them

    A normalized words frame from load_scanpath_data.

  • fixations (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    A normalized fixations frame.

  • raw_gaze (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

plot_scanpath(
    words=None,
    fixations=None,
    participant=None,
    trial=None,
    *,
    screen=None,
    canvas_size=None,
    base_font_size=16,
    font_family=FONT_FAMILY,
    raw_gaze=None,
    drift_correction=None,
    drift_connectors=False,
    fix_index_range=None,
    illustration=False,
    illustration_label="auto",
    title="",
    caption="",
    column_names=None,
    **figure_overrides,
)

Build one trial's scanpath figure, by default in the app's Scanpath design.

Every figure option is a keyword (show_heatmap=True, color_by="pass_index", x_field="order_in_trial"), and figure_options lists them with their defaults. An option naming a column takes either name: frames under the dataset's own column names, as load_scanpath_data returns them by default, are read through the map they carry.

Parameters:

  • words (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    A normalized words frame from load_scanpath_data, or None for a dataset recorded as raw gaze alone.

  • fixations (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    The normalized fixations frame, or None likewise.

  • participant (str | None, default: None ) –

    The participant id. It may be left out when the frames hold one trial.

  • trial (str | None, default: None ) –

    The trial id. It may be left out when the frames hold one trial.

  • screen (str | None, default: None ) –

    The screen of a multipart trial to draw. Left out, the first recorded screen; coordinate spaces are never concatenated.

  • canvas_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    The monitor size in px, (width, height). Estimated from the data's extent by default; pass the real resolution ((2560, 1440) for OneStop) to keep coordinates true to scale.

  • base_font_size (int, default: 16 ) –

    The base font size in px.

  • font_family (str, default: FONT_FAMILY ) –

    The font family.

  • raw_gaze (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    Samples from load_raw_gaze, filtered to the trial and drawn as recorded, under the fixations. It can be the only table: with words and fixations None, the trial is looked up in the samples, the canvas is estimated from their extent, and the figure is the samples alone. No fixations are detected from them, so the fixation, saccade and heatmap layers stay empty.

  • drift_correction (str | None, default: None ) –

    Experimental. Without SCANPATH_EXPERIMENTAL=1, anything but None or "off" raises ValueError.

  • drift_connectors (bool, default: False ) –

    Experimental, with drift_correction.

  • fix_index_range (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    (start, end): draw only fixations start to end of the trial, 1-based and both inclusive. The app's fixation-index window.

  • illustration (bool, default: False ) –

    Apply the Illustration preset: fixations snapped to their lines, arced saccades, uniform colors, no heatmap or word boxes. Keywords you pass still win.

  • illustration_label (str, default: 'auto' ) –

    "auto" labels the figure an illustration when it no longer shows the data as recorded; "show" and "hide" decide it.

  • title (str, default: '' ) –

    A title band stamped onto the figure without shrinking the plot, like the app's Title & labels. Literal text, not the app's {trial_id}-style pattern, since you know which trial it is.

  • caption (str, default: '' ) –

    A caption band, likewise.

  • column_names (dict | None, default: None ) –

    The column map for frames loaded with names="canonical" (data.column_names). The options then take the dataset's names too, and the figure's text uses them.

  • **figure_overrides (Any, default: {} ) –

    Any figure option, in place of the app's default. Three take a word of explanation:

    • palette= ("default", "print" or "high-contrast", or the app's names) sets a group of colors at once. A color you pass explicitly wins.
    • show_stimulus_image=True draws the trial's own stimulus page under the scanpath, as the app's 📄 Stimulus → image does: the image_path its rows carry (from load_scanpath_data(image_root=…) or attach_stimulus_images; the demo ships its pages), at its image_x / image_y. A background_image= you pass wins.
    • fixation_snap_to_line=True moves each fixation up or down onto its text line, keeping its x: its word's line, else the nearest. fixation_snap_position says where, in line heights from the line's middle (default −0.5, its top edge). The saccades' ends move with the markers, and it does nothing with show_fixations=False.

Returns:

  • Figure –

    The Plotly figure.

Raises:

  • TypeError –

    An unknown keyword. The message names the closest valid ones.

  • ValueError –

    A value an enumerated option does not take, or a color_by / highlight_column naming a column the trial's table doesn't have. The message names the closest ones.

Warns:

  • UserWarning –

    show_stimulus_image=True on a trial with no readable page (a PNG). The figure draws none.

animate_scanpath(
    words=None,
    fixations=None,
    participant=None,
    trial=None,
    *,
    screen=None,
    screen_b=None,
    canvas_size=None,
    base_font_size=16,
    font_family=FONT_FAMILY,
    playback_speed=1.0,
    autoplay=True,
    fix_index_range=None,
    fix_index_range_b=None,
    illustration_label="auto",
    title="",
    caption="",
    column_names=None,
    trial_b=None,
    dataset_b=None,
    setup=None,
    setup_b=None,
    **animation_overrides,
)

Build the animated replay of one trial's scanpath, or of two on one clock.

Save it as interactive HTML with save_figure, whose page keeps the replay's clock itself, or rasterize it to GIF or MP4 with animation_export.export_animation, which lasts as long. fig.show() plays it on Plotly's own frame queue, which runs slow.

The replay takes a subset of plot_scanpath's options (figure_options("animation")), and the ones they share default alike, so the replay matches the static figure. The replay is made of fixations: it draws no raw gaze, and nothing detects fixations from samples.

Two scanpaths. trial_b co-animates a second trial, like the app's Animate + Compare. Both readings are drawn in A's coordinates, so a co-animation is an overlay, and a trial from another dataset has to share A's screen. Name that dataset with dataset_b (or give its setup_b), and the pair is checked the way compare_scanpaths checks an overlay. B's frames passed without either are taken to be from A's dataset, as render passes them for --compare-with alone, and are not checked: two readings of one corpus can span different extents, and inferring a canvas from each would refuse pairs that shared a screen.

Parameters:

  • words (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • fixations (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • participant (str | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • trial (str | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • screen (str | None, default: None ) –

    A's screen of a multipart trial, as in plot_scanpath.

  • screen_b (str | None, default: None ) –

    B's screen, looked up in B's own trial. Left out, its first recorded screen.

  • canvas_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    A's monitor size, as in plot_scanpath.

  • base_font_size (int, default: 16 ) –

    The base font size in px.

  • font_family (str, default: FONT_FAMILY ) –

    The font family.

  • playback_speed (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    The replay lasts the reading time divided by this. Any other value than 1 makes the automatic Illustration label say the timing was changed.

  • autoplay (bool, default: True ) –

    Start the saved HTML's replay when it opens, at playback_speed. False saves it paused, to start with ▶ Play. A GIF or MP4 always plays from its first frame.

  • fix_index_range (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    (start, end): replay only that window of the trial's fixations, 1-based and inclusive. In a co-animation it windows A only, as in the app, where A's slider never cuts B.

  • fix_index_range_b (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    B's window, in a co-animation.

  • illustration_label (str, default: 'auto' ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • title (str, default: '' ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • caption (str, default: '' ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • column_names (dict | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • trial_b (tuple[str, str] | None, default: None ) –

    B's (participant, trial). It is looked up in words_b / fixations_b when they are given, else in words / fixations, as compare_scanpaths takes it.

  • dataset_b (str | None, default: None ) –

    The name of B's dataset, when it is another one. The pair is then checked as an overlay, and B's participant ids are prefixed with it, so a hover says whose participant it is.

  • setup (SetupSnapshot | None, default: None ) –

    A's experimental_setup.SetupSnapshot, the screen the overlay check reads. A side without one is read off its data: the extent of that one trial, which rarely spans the whole screen, so state both when you know them.

  • setup_b (SetupSnapshot | None, default: None ) –

    B's.

  • **animation_overrides (Any, default: {} ) –

    Any figure option the replay takes. Also:

    • words_b / fixations_b: B's frames. Without trial_b they must hold one trial.
    • style_a / style_b: each scanpath's style, with the keys compare_scanpaths takes for markers and saccades (fix_color, marker_size_range, opacity, hollow, saccade_color, saccade_style, saccade_width), so the replay and the static comparison draw each trial alike. A lone replay ignores them.
    • fixation_flags_b: B's own fixation flags. None uses A's fixation_flags, or style_b's when it names some.
    • show_stimulus_image=True draws the trial's own page, as in plot_scanpath. A co-animation draws one page, under the text it draws: B's when compare_stimulus="b", else A's.
    • palette= works here too. Colors it implies that the replay doesn't take are dropped rather than raising, since you named a look, not those keys.

Returns:

  • Figure –

    The animated Plotly figure.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    The trial has no fixations (one recorded as raw gaze alone, or a words-only one). Also for raw_gaze=; draw samples with plot_scanpath(raw_gaze=…).

  • ValueError –

    An option the replay does not take (the message names the valid ones), a style naming saccade_classes (the replay has no saccade-class filter), or B frames holding several trials without trial_b.

  • IncomparableScreensError –

    B's dataset has a different canvas from A's. A ValueError.

compare_scanpaths(
    words,
    fixations,
    trial_a,
    trial_b,
    *,
    screen=None,
    screen_b=None,
    words_b=None,
    fixations_b=None,
    dataset_b="Dataset B",
    raw_gaze=None,
    raw_gaze_b=None,
    layout="overlay",
    compare_stimulus="both",
    setup=None,
    setup_b=None,
    canvas_size=None,
    labels=None,
    style_a=None,
    style_b=None,
    base_font_size=16,
    font_family=FONT_FAMILY,
    fix_index_range=None,
    fix_index_range_b=None,
    drift_correction=None,
    title="",
    caption="",
    column_names=None,
    **figure_overrides,
)

Build a figure comparing two scanpaths: the app's Compare mode.

Multipart trials. Each scanpath is one screen, never a whole multipart trial: every screen is its own coordinate space, so pooling them would draw saccades across page boundaries. list_parts() lists the screens.

Two datasets. words_b / fixations_b draw B from a different dataset. Two datasets can hold the same (participant_id, trial_id), so B's participant ids are namespaced with dataset_b inside the merged frames; without that, one trial would silently render as two. The frames you pass in are never modified, and only the trace labels show the namespace.

The overlay gate. An overlay needs both readings on screens of the same size, or it raises ValueError (the app falls back to side by side). That holds across datasets, and within one when the two screens carry different canvas_width / canvas_height or setup_b states another screen. Pass layout="side_by_side" or "stacked" to compare readings from different screens; each panel is then drawn to its own. Nothing is rescaled.

Per-scanpath style. style_a / style_b restyle one scanpath with these keys:

Key What it sets Left out fix_color, saccade_color The scanpath's colors Its default marker_size_range, opacity, hollow Its fixation markers Its default saccade_style, saccade_width Its saccade lines Its default box_color The outline of that reading's word boxes Its fix_color box_fill_color Their fill word_box_fill_color box_line_opacity, box_fill_opacity Their outline's and fill's opacity, 0–1 (0 hides it) word_box_line_opacity, word_box_fill_opacity raw_gaze_color That reading's raw-gaze samples Its fix_color heatmap_colorscale That reading's word-box heatmap color scale, on the range both share; two different scales get a color bar each heatmap_colorscale fixation_flags, saccade_classes That scanpath's own filters, in place of the figure's The figure's

The box keys and raw_gaze_color are this figure's only: the co-animation draws one set of boxes and no raw gaze, and ignores them.

Parameters:

  • words (DataFrame) –

    The words frame holding both trials, or A's when words_b is given.

  • fixations (DataFrame) –

    The fixations frame, likewise.

  • trial_a (tuple[str, str]) –

    A's (participant, trial).

  • trial_b (tuple[str, str]) –

    B's (participant, trial).

  • screen (str | None, default: None ) –

    A's screen of a multipart trial. Left out, its first recorded screen, as in plot_scanpath.

  • screen_b (str | None, default: None ) –

    B's screen, looked up in B's own frames, so it may be a later page or another dataset's.

  • words_b (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    B's words frame, to draw B from another dataset.

  • fixations_b (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    B's fixations frame, likewise.

  • dataset_b (str, default: 'Dataset B' ) –

    The name B's participant ids are namespaced with.

  • raw_gaze (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    Samples from load_raw_gaze, drawn under each reading's scanpath in its color. It serves both readings of one dataset; across datasets it is A's. Passing it turns the layer on; show_raw_gaze=False keeps it off.

  • raw_gaze_b (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    B's samples, across datasets.

  • layout (str, default: 'overlay' ) –

    "overlay", "side_by_side" ("side-by-side" also works) or "stacked".

  • compare_stimulus (str, default: 'both' ) –

    Whose word boxes and text an overlay draws: "both", "a" or "b". Two datasets' boxes coincide only when the text is identical. Split layouts ignore it, since each panel draws its own.

  • setup (SetupSnapshot | None, default: None ) –

    A's experimental_setup.SetupSnapshot, the screen the overlay gate reads.

  • setup_b (SetupSnapshot | None, default: None ) –

    B's.

  • canvas_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    A's monitor size, when you only have a resolution. Left out with setup, the canvas is read off the data.

  • labels (tuple[str, str] | None, default: None ) –

    The two trace labels, when not the composed defaults.

  • style_a (dict | None, default: None ) –

    A's style, with the keys above.

  • style_b (dict | None, default: None ) –

    B's style.

  • base_font_size (int, default: 16 ) –

    The base font size in px.

  • font_family (str, default: FONT_FAMILY ) –

    The font family.

  • fix_index_range (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    (start, end): draw only that window of both scanpaths' fixations.

  • fix_index_range_b (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    B's own window, as the app's B slider sets it.

  • drift_correction (str | None, default: None ) –

    Experimental, as in plot_scanpath.

  • title (str, default: '' ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • caption (str, default: '' ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • column_names (dict | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath. A's names, or column_names, name the options and the figure's text; either dataset's frames may come under their own names.

  • **figure_overrides (Any, default: {} ) –

    Any figure option a comparison takes (figure_options("comparison")). Some act per scanpath:

    • fixation_flags and saccade_classes filter both scanpaths, unless a style gives one its own.
    • background_image is A's page. A split layout draws B's panel over background_image_b (with background_image_size_b / background_image_origin_b), and over nothing without it, never A's, since sharing a dataset says nothing about sharing a page.
    • show_stimulus_image=True takes each reading's own page from its rows: a split layout draws A's and B's, each in its panel, and an overlay the page of the text it draws (B's for compare_stimulus="b", else A's). An image passed explicitly wins.

Returns:

  • Figure –

    The Plotly figure.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    An overlay of two different screens (see the overlay gate), or a screen / screen_b the trial does not have or that names a screen of a single-screen trial.

  • TypeError –

    An unknown keyword. The message names the closest valid ones.

figure_options(kind='static', *, choices=False)

List every figure keyword a builder takes, with the default it renders with.

The defaults are what a call actually renders with, the app's Scanpath design, so a script can diff its intended settings against what it would get. The Figure options page of these docs lists them by section, with their render flags.

docs.title: Reproduce a figure in code
docs.text:
The app's Share subtab shows the API or CLI code that rebuilds the figure currently on screen — paste it into a notebook or terminal to get the same figure. figure_code is the headless form of that block, and render --print-code prints it for an invocation you already have.

print(
    sps.figure_code(
        participant="l7_1090",
        trial="l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele_r0",
        show_heatmap=True,
        color_by="duration_ms",
    )
)

import scanpath_studio as sps

words, fixations = sps.load_sample_data()

fig = sps.plot_scanpath(
    words,
    fixations,
    participant='l7_1090',
    trial='l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele_r0',
    canvas_size=(2560, 1440),
    color_by='duration_ms',
    show_heatmap=True,
)

sps.save_figure(fig, 'scanpath.png')

Give it the arguments you would give plot_scanpath (kind="static"), animate_scanpath ("animation") or compare_scanpaths ("comparison"), and it returns the snippet that rebuilds that figure. Only the options that differ from figure_options are written, so the snippet stays readable. code_snippet.ReproductionCode is the structured form.

    "static", "animation" or "comparison": the builder the snippet calls.

  • source (str, default: 'demo' ) –

    How the data is loaded: "demo", "synthetic", "files", "potec", "onestop", "author", "raw_gaze" (a dataset recorded as raw gaze alone, whose samples at source_options["raw_gaze"] are the data), or "unknown" for data a snippet can't name.

    A's screen of a multipart trial (screen=, --screen).

    B's (participant, trial), for a comparison or a co-animation.

  • compare_screen (str | None, default: None ) –

    B's screen (screen_b=, --compare-screen).

  • compare_layout (str, default: 'overlay' ) –

    The comparison's layout, as compare_scanpaths takes it.

  • compare_stimulus (str, default: 'both' ) –

    Whose stimulus an overlay draws, as compare_scanpaths takes it.

  • compare_dataset (str, default: '' ) –

    The dataset B was loaded from, when it is a second one. Both forms then load B's own tables, from the placeholder paths B_WORDS / B_FIXATIONS that you point at its files (words_b= / fixations_b= / dataset_b=, and --compare-words / --compare-fixations).

  • compare_canvas (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    B's screen, (width, height), with compare_dataset: written as setup_b= and --compare-canvas, which a co-animation across datasets needs.

  • compare_labels (tuple[str, str] | None, default: None ) –

    The two trace labels, when they are not the composed defaults: labels= and --label-a / --label-b.

  • canvas_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    The monitor size. Defaults to the screen render assumes for the source (the demo's 2560×1440, PoTeC's 1680×1050, …), so both forms draw the same figure.

  • base_font_size (int, default: 16 ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • font_family (str, default: FONT_FAMILY ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • title (str, default: '' ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • caption (str, default: '' ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • fix_index_range (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • illustration_label (str, default: 'auto' ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • drift_correction (str | None, default: None ) –

    Experimental, as in plot_scanpath.

  • drift_connectors (bool, default: False ) –

    Experimental, as in plot_scanpath.

  • playback_speed (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    As animate_scanpath takes it.

  • autoplay (bool, default: True ) –

    As animate_scanpath takes it.

  • flavor (str, default: 'python' ) –

    "python", "cli", or "both" (separated by a blank line).

  • explicit (bool, default: False ) –

    Write every option at its current value, not only the ones that differ from the defaults.

  • output (str | None, default: None ) –

    The file the snippet saves. Defaults to scanpath.html for an animation (render --animate writes only HTML) and to a PNG otherwise.

    The figure options, as the builder takes them.

Returns:

  • str –

    The snippet. Anything neither form can reproduce (a raw-gaze table with no path to name, an uploaded stimulus image, B's rows from a second corpus) follows as # Note: comments, as the app's ⚠️ captions and the Note: lines render --print-code writes to stderr say it.

  • TypeError –

    An option the builder does not take.

Examples:

    sps.figure_code(
        participant="l7_1090",
        trial="l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele_r0",
        show_heatmap=True,
        flavor="cli",
    )
)

docs.title: cache_status
docs.text:
cache_status()

Describe the recovery cache a local run keeps, without launching the app.

A local or desktop app stores completed uploaded datasets, column mappings, view settings, saved designs, metadata tables and annotations under your cache folder, so a refresh or a restart resumes where it left off. A hosted deployment never does. The same information is in the app's 🗂️ Data Management → Saved on this computer, and in scanpath-studio cache.

Key What it holds enabled, directory Whether caching is on, and where exists, readable Whether its manifest is there and can be read datasets Each stored dataset's name and per-frame row counts rows, bytes, saved_at The totals, and when it was last written annotations, designs, metadata, settings What else is stored damaged Each stored dataset whose entry or files are broken, with the reason. The app restores the others and keeps that one rather than dropping it damaged_metadata Why the stored metadata tables would not restore; "" when they would

Returns:

  • dict –

    The status, as a dict with the keys above. Delete the cache with clear_cache.

docs.title: clear_cache
docs.text:
clear_cache()

Delete the recovery cache.

Removes only the files the app wrote (manifest.json and the datasets' Parquet files); anything else in the folder is left alone. A running local app writes its session back out at its next change, so start it with scanpath-studio run --no-persist or SCANPATH_STUDIO_PERSIST=0 to stop that.

Returns:

  • dict –

    The cache's status afterwards, as cache_status gives it.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
scanpath-studio launches the app. Its subcommands do the rest without opening it:

Command What it does scanpath-studio, run Launch the app render Write one trial's scanpath, heatmap or replay to a file corpus Render a corpus figure from a tidy CSV you already have check Run the Data checks on your tables cache Show or clear the recovery cache version Show the build, and whether a newer release is out

Each command takes --help, and scanpath-studio --version prints the version. A word that is not a command is an error naming the closest one, rather than an argument passed on to Streamlit.

docs.title: Launch the app
docs.text:
scanpath-studio
scanpath-studio --server.port 8600
scanpath-studio --no-persist          # don't cache the session on this computer
scanpath-studio --download-dir D:\corpora  # where ⬇ Download saves public datasets

scanpath-studio run … is the same. Any other launch flag is passed on to streamlit run.

The app listens on this computer only (127.0.0.1). It has no login, so serving it to other machines is a deliberate step. Pass --server.address 0.0.0.0 (or set server.address in a Streamlit config.toml, or STREAMLIT_SERVER_ADDRESS), and only on a network you trust:

scanpath-studio --server.address 0.0.0.0

Served on a network, the app also turns off everything that reads or writes the server's own folders, since any visitor could use them: the Data directory box, the folder picker, and ⬇ Download for the public corpora and stimulus-image folders. On a lab server you trust, turn them back on with SCANPATH_LOCAL_FS=1 (SCANPATH_LOCAL_FS=1 scanpath-studio --server.address 0.0.0.0).

docs.title: render
docs.text:
render writes one trial to a file without opening the app. The extension picks the format: .html is interactive and needs nothing else, while .png, .svg and .pdf need Chrome, Chromium or Edge (or run plotly_get_chrome -y once; see the FAQ). The figure is the app's Scanpath design unless a flag changes it, and every figure option has a flag.

# The trials there are to pick from
scanpath-studio render --sample --list-trials

# The bundled demo
scanpath-studio render --sample -o scanpath.html

# Your own data (replace p1 / t3 with ids from --list-trials)
scanpath-studio render \
  --words ia.csv --fixations fixations.csv \
  --participant p1 --trial t3 --output scanpath.svg

# An authoring file saved from the app's Author a scanpath screen
scanpath-studio render --authoring authored-scanpath.json -o authored.html

# A public corpus, loaded the way the app loads it (PoTeC downloads on first use)
scanpath-studio render --potec ./potec --list-trials
scanpath-studio render --onestop ./onestop --onestop-variant public \
  --onestop-regime ordinary --onestop-part Paragraph --list-trials

The Python API loads the same corpora with load_potec and load_onestop.

docs.title: Common tasks
docs.text: Goal Flags add a layer --word-boxes, --fixation-index, --heatmap hide a layer --no-text, --no-fixations, --no-saccades animate --animate, optionally --playback-speed X. Every styling flag the replay can draw is honored; the rest are named in a warning set the display geometry --canvas WIDTHxHEIGHT. --crop-to-data frames the data instead of the whole monitor, with --crop-margin PX around it (default: 5% of its extent, at least 20 px) color fixations --color-by FIELD, including a column of your own once --keep-columns COLUMN… carries it through loading size fixations by duration --marker-size-scale sqrt\|linear\|log\|relative (default sqrt), --marker-duration-range LO HI (ms, default 50 600), --marker-size-range MIN MAX (px), --no-duration-size-legend draw only part of a trial --fix-index-range START:END (1-based, both inclusive; --animate and --compare-with honor it too) draw the stimulus --stimulus-image PATH for one image. --show-stimulus-image draws each trial's own page, the image_path its rows carry (--sample ships its pages). --image-root DIR --image-pattern '{text_id}.png' fills image_path from a folder smooth the heatmap --heatmap-style interpolated --heatmap-sigma 20 (σ in px; leave it out for an automatic σ) style the word boxes --word-box-color, --word-box-line-opacity, --word-box-fill-color, --word-box-fill-opacity (0 draws outlines only, or fill only) size the figure --width, --height, --scale. For print, --width-mm MM or --width-in IN with --dpi N (default 300) title and caption it --title, --caption export editable layers --separable-layers print the equivalent code --print-code python (or cli / both), plus --print-code-explicit

docs.title: Compare two scanpaths
docs.text:
--compare-with PARTICIPANT:TRIAL draws a second trial, B, beside or over the first. It is the headless form of the app's Compare mode.

# Two participants on the same paragraph, overlaid
scanpath-studio render --sample -p l37_1129 -t l37_1129_2_1_1_Ele_r0 \
  --compare-with l7_1090:l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele_r0 -o compare.html

# The same overlay, drawing only B's word boxes and text
scanpath-studio render --sample -p l37_1129 -t l37_1129_2_1_1_Ele_r0 \
  --compare-with l7_1090:l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele_r0 --compare-stimulus b \
  -o compare_b.html

# Side by side: each panel draws its own trial's stimulus
scanpath-studio render --sample -p l37_1129 -t l37_1129_2_1_1_Ele_r0 \
  --compare-with l7_1090:l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele_r0 \
  --compare-layout side-by-side -o compare.svg

# Each scanpath styled
scanpath-studio render --sample -p l37_1129 -t l37_1129_2_1_1_Ele_r0 \
  --compare-with l7_1090:l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele_r0 \
  --style-a fix_color=#D55E00,opacity=0.5 --style-b saccade_style=dash \
  -o compare_styled.html

# B from a second dataset
scanpath-studio render --words ia.csv --fixations fix.csv -p p1 -t t1 \
  --compare-with p1:t1 \
  --compare-words other/ia.csv --compare-fixations other/fix.csv \
  --compare-dataset-name "Our lab" \
  --canvas 1680x1050 --compare-canvas 1680x1050 \
  -o cross.html
Goal Flags pick B --compare-with PARTICIPANT:TRIAL pick each screen of a multipart trial --screen ID (A), --compare-screen ID (B); each defaults to its trial's first screen arrange the panels --compare-layout {overlay,side-by-side,stacked} (default overlay) choose whose stimulus an overlay draws --compare-stimulus {both,a,b} (default both) name the two scanpaths --label-a TEXT --label-b TEXT (both or neither) style each scanpath --style-a SPEC, --style-b SPEC (keys below) leave out the A/B legend --no-compare-legend give B its own stimulus page (split layouts) --stimulus-image-b PATH, with --stimulus-image-size-b WxH / --stimulus-image-origin-b X,Y take B from another dataset --compare-words PATH… --compare-fixations PATH…, plus --compare-raw-gaze PATH… and --compare-dataset-name NAME declare the screens --canvas WxH, --compare-canvas WxH replay both on one clock add --animate (HTML output)

--label-a / --label-b and --style-a / --style-b apply to the --animate replay too.

docs.title: Style keys
docs.text:
--style-a and --style-b take a comma-separated KEY=VALUE list and can be repeated. They are the app's Scanpath A / Scanpath B rows and compare_scanpaths's style_a / style_b. A key left out keeps that scanpath's default.

Key Value Left out fix_color #RRGGBB that scanpath's default saccade_color #RRGGBB that scanpath's default box_color #RRGGBB, the outline of that scanpath's word boxes its fix_color box_fill_color #RRGGBB, the boxes' fill --word-box-fill-color box_line_opacity, box_fill_opacity 0–1 --word-box-line-opacity, --word-box-fill-opacity raw_gaze_color #RRGGBB, that scanpath's raw-gaze samples its fix_color heatmap_colorscale a Plotly color scale; the range stays shared, and two different scales get a color bar each --heatmap-colorscale saccade_style solid, dash, dot or dashdot that scanpath's default saccade_width px that scanpath's default marker_size_range MIN:MAX that scanpath's default opacity 0.1–1 that scanpath's default hollow true or false that scanpath's default

The --animate replay draws one set of word boxes and no raw gaze, so it ignores the box_* keys and raw_gaze_color.

docs.title: What a comparison can't combine
docs.text:
• --compare-with cannot be combined with --all-screens or --screens. A comparison is one figure of two trials, each drawn from one screen. B's --compare-screen is looked up in B's own trial, so it can be a later page, or a page of the second dataset.
  • An overlay of two datasets needs matching canvases. On two different canvases, --compare-layout overlay fails rather than falling back, and so does --animate, which replays both scanpaths in one coordinate space. Use --compare-layout side-by-side or stacked, without --animate. Two screens of one dataset whose canvases differ are refused the same way. Nothing is rescaled.
  • Without --compare-canvas, the second dataset's screen is read off its data, as A's is when neither --canvas nor a built-in source gives one. That extent rarely spans the whole screen, so state both screens when you know them.
  • A second dataset is loaded from files only. Any corpus you can load in Python can still be B through compare_scanpaths, which takes B's frames directly.

docs.title: Raw gaze
docs.text:
--raw-gaze PATH… reads a third table, with its columns auto-detected like --fixations, and draws the plotted trial's samples under the fixations. With --compare-with it covers both scanpaths, each in its own color, and --compare-raw-gaze PATH… is B's when B comes from another dataset. --animate ignores it with a warning.

scanpath-studio render --sample -p l37_1129 -t l37_1129_2_2_2_Adv_r0 \
  --sample-raw-gaze --raw-gaze-opacity 0.4 -o raw_gaze.html

On its own, with no other input, --raw-gaze is the dataset: --list-trials lists its trials and render draws the chosen trial's samples as recorded. No fixations are detected from them, so --animate and --compare-with exit with that reason instead.

scanpath-studio render --raw-gaze gaze_samples.csv --list-trials
scanpath-studio render --raw-gaze gaze_samples.csv -t t3 -o samples.png

docs.title: Multipart trials and many trials
docs.text:
render writes one trial per run. For many figures, use the Python batch recipe or the app's Export → Export bundle.

A multipart trial is the exception. --all-screens writes one __screen-001-<id> file per screen of the selected trial, and --screens Title,Paragraph writes only the screens named, each still numbered by its place in the trial. --trial-parts-manifest manifest.json assigns arbitrary source rows to screens.

scanpath-studio render --words ia.csv --fixations fix.csv --list-parts
scanpath-studio render --words ia.csv --fixations fix.csv \
  -p p1 -t t3 --screen question -o question.svg
scanpath-studio render --words ia.csv --fixations fix.csv \
  -p p1 -t t3 --all-screens --animate --screen-transition recorded \
  -o replay.html

docs.title: When a column isn't recognized
docs.text:
Column names are auto-detected (EyeLink, Tobii, SMI, Pupil Labs, Gazepoint and snake_case spellings). When one isn't, render stops and prints which field it could not find, the names it looked for, the columns your table has, and a mapping to start from. Pass that mapping back as JSON, inline or as a path to a .json file, with --word-schema (the --words table) and/or --fix-schema (the --fixations table). check takes the same two flags.

scanpath-studio render --words ia.csv --fixations fix.csv \
  --word-schema '{"trial": "TRIAL_LABEL", "word_id": "IA_ID", "text": "IA_LABEL",
                  "left": "IA_LEFT", "right": "IA_RIGHT", "top": "IA_TOP", "bottom": "IA_BOTTOM"}' \
  --fix-schema fix_schema.json -o scanpath.html

A mapping replaces auto-detection for that table, so it has to name every required field, not only the one that failed. It is the same dict load_scanpath_data(word_schema=…, fix_schema=…) takes in Python.

docs.title: render flags
docs.text: Every render flag, generated from the parser the command uses, so the defaults and help are the ones --help prints. The figure flags are grouped like the figure options they set.

docs.title: Trial and output
docs.text: Option Value Default Description -p--participant PARTICIPANT — Participant id (default: first available). -t--trial TRIAL — Trial id (default: first for the participant). --screen SCREEN — Screen/part id inside a multipart trial (default: first screen). --list-trials switch — Print every trial (participant, trial and text id) and exit; pass the trial id to -t. --list-parts switch — Print ordered multipart screens, optionally narrowed by -p/-t, and exit. --all-screens switch — Render every screen of the selected parent trial. Screen ids are inserted before the output extension. --screens ID[,ID...] — Like --all-screens, but only these screens of the parent trial (comma-separated screen ids, e.g. Title,Paragraph); see --list-parts. --screen-transition instant, recorded instant For --all-screens --animate, record zero or observed inter-screen delay in each output's metadata (default: instant). -o--output PATH — Output file; format from extension (.html/.png/.svg/.pdf). --animate switch — Render the animated replay instead of the static figure (HTML only).

docs.title: Input
docs.text: Option Value Default Description --sample switch — Use the bundled OneStop demo: 2 participants, 12 trials each (--list-trials shows them). --authoring PATH — An authoring file from the app's Author a scanpath screen. --words PATH [PATH ...] — Words table(s) (csv/tsv/txt/tab/parquet/feather/xlsx/xls, or a .zip of them); columns are auto-detected from EyeLink, Gazepoint, Tobii, SMI, Pupil Labs and snake_case names. Multiple paths or a quoted glob pattern concatenate multi-file datasets. --fixations PATH [PATH ...] — Fixations table(s) (csv/tsv/txt/tab/parquet/feather/xlsx/xls, or a .zip of them), auto-detected like --words. Multiple paths or a quoted glob pattern concatenate multi-file datasets (e.g. one file per participant). --image-root DIR — Local stimulus-image folder. Files are matched per row using --image-pattern and fill its image_path; add --show-stimulus-image to draw them. Works with every input, --sample and the corpora included. --image-pattern PATTERN {text_id}.png Relative filename pattern with row placeholders, for example '{text_id}.png' or '{participant_id}/{trial_id}.png'. --trial-parts-manifest PATH — JSON manifest that assigns arbitrary source rows to ordered screens inside each logical trial. Use with --words/--fixations when the source tables have no explicit screen columns. --word-schema JSON — Column mapping for the --words table, replacing auto-detection: a JSON object (or a path to a .json file holding one) from each field to a column name, e.g. '{"trial": "TRIAL_INDEX", "word_id": "IA_ID", ...}' — the same dict api.load_scanpath_data takes. Needed only when a column isn't recognized; the error then prints a mapping to start from. --fix-schema JSON — Column mapping for the --fixations table, replacing auto-detection: a JSON object (or a path to a .json file holding one) from each field to a column name, e.g. '{"trial": "TRIAL_INDEX", "word_id": "IA_ID", ...}' — the same dict api.load_scanpath_data takes. Needed only when a column isn't recognized; the error then prints a mapping to start from. --keep-columns COLUMN [COLUMN ...] — Further columns of your own to carry through loading under their own names (e.g. a pupil size), from whichever table has them — otherwise loading keeps only the mapped and recognized fields. A kept fixation column can then be --color-by, an axis or a hover field. The keep_columns= of api.load_scanpath_data. --potec DIR — Load the PoTeC corpus (DiLi-Lab/PoTeC) from DIR, downloading the needed files (~45 MB) on first use. Participants are the corpus's 75 ids (sparse within 0–105; --list-trials shows them); a trial is one participant reading one text, <participant>_<text> (0_b0), with texts b0–b5 and p0–p5. --onestop DIR — Load the OneStop corpus from DIR. For the public variant the chosen regime + parts' reports are downloaded from OSF on first use (tens–hundreds MB each); the lacclab variant reads a local export. Tune with --onestop-regime / --onestop-part / --onestop-variant. --onestop-regime ordinary, information_seeking, repeated, information_seeking_repeated ordinary OneStop reading regime for --onestop (default: ordinary). --onestop-part Title, Question_Preview, Paragraph, Questions, Answers, QA, Feedback — OneStop trial part(s) for --onestop; repeatable (default: Paragraph). Loading several makes each part its own trial. --onestop-variant public, lacclab public OneStop source variant for --onestop: 'public' (OSF download) or 'lacclab' (a local lab-processed export; no download). --participant-metadata FILE [FILE ...] — Participant-level metadata table: one row per participant, an id column plus anything known about them. Several files (or a glob) are stacked into one table. The join is validated and reported against the loaded participants, and the fields are added to --list-trials output. --trial-metadata FILE [FILE ...] — Trial-level metadata table: one row per trial, a trial-id column plus anything known about it. Several files (or a glob) are stacked into one table. Validated and reported the same way, and its fields are added to --list-trials output. --trial-metadata-participant-column--trial-metadata-reader-column COLUMN — Key the --trial-metadata table by participant AND trial, using this column as the participant id. Without it the table is keyed by trial id alone: a row describes a text, and every trial of it inherits that row. Never inferred: nothing in the file says which of the two a corpus means. --text-metadata FILE [FILE ...] — Text-level metadata table: one row per text, a text-id column plus anything known about it. Several files (or a glob) are stacked into one table. Validated and reported the same way, and its fields are added to --list-trials output. Never keyed by participant: a text is a stimulus, not something one participant owns.

docs.title: Fixations
docs.text: Option Value Default Description --no-fixations switch — Hide fixation markers. --fixation-index switch — Number the fixations in reading order. --no-fixation-index--no-order switch — Hide the fixation numbers (the default). --fix-index-range START:END — Draw only fixations START through END of the trial (1-based, both inclusive), e.g. --fix-index-range 1:40. Honored by --animate too, which then replays only that window, and by --compare-with, which windows both scanpaths (unless --compare-fix-index-range gives B its own). --fixation-flag SPEC — The app's Filters & highlights for fixations, repeatable. SPEC is CATEGORY=MODE[,threshold_ms=N][,symbol=S][,color=#RRGGBB] with CATEGORY one of short, long, oob (outside every word box), blink and MODE one of off, highlight, discard — e.g. --fixation-flag short=discard,threshold_ms=80. discard drops those fixations from the drawing only; measures and exports are untouched. threshold_ms applies to short/long only. --snap-fixations switch — Move each fixation up or down onto its text line (its word's, else the nearest); it keeps its x. --snap-position says where on the line. --snap-position LINES — Where on its line a snapped fixation sits, in line heights from the line's middle: 0 centers it, -0.5 is the top edge, 0.5 the bottom edge (default: -0.5). Used with --snap-fixations. --palette {default,print,high-contrast} — Color palette for the marks (the app's Palette): default (colorblind-safe, Okabe–Ito), print (grayscale, survives a B&W print) or high-contrast. The app's own names work too. Individual --*-color flags override it. --color-by FIELD — Fixation column to color by, e.g. duration_ms, or 'line' to color each fixation by its text line (same as --color-by-line). Default: '(uniform)', one flat color, since marker size already shows duration. --fixation-color COLOR — Flat fixation marker color used when --color-by is (uniform) (default: #0072B2). --fixation-symbol circle, square, diamond, triangle-up, cross, x, star, hexagon, heart — Fixation marker shape. Unlike color, shape survives a grayscale print (default: circle). --fixation-colorscale NAME — Color scale for --color-by, e.g. Viridis (default: Blues). --marker-size-range MIN MAX — Min/max fixation marker size in px, e.g. 4 12 (default: 8 24). Smaller ranges suit small thumbnails. --marker-size-scale sqrt, linear, log, relative — How duration sets marker size (default: sqrt). sqrt / linear / log map --marker-duration-range onto --marker-size-range the same way for every figure, so one duration is one size across trials, comparisons and replays; sqrt makes marker area grow with duration. relative stretches each figure from its own shortest to longest fixation. --marker-duration-range LO HI — Durations in ms given the smallest and largest marker on a fixed scale (default: 50 600). Shorter and longer fixations clamp to them. --fixation-opacity O — Fixation marker opacity, 0.1–1.0 (default: 0.7, so overlapping fixations show through). --fixation-outline-width PX — Outline round each filled fixation marker, 0–5 px; 0 draws none (default: 0.5). --fixation-outline-color COLOR — Color of that outline (default: #111111). --hollow-fixations switch — Draw the fixations as outlines instead of filled markers. --color-by-line switch — Color each fixation by the text line it lands on (lines inferred from the word boxes); overrides --color-by. Same as --color-by line. --fixation-color-range LO HI — Pin the --color-by color scale to LO..HI instead of the trial's own range, so several figures share one scale. --order-font-size PX — Fixation index label size (default: 10). --order-font-color COLOR — Fixation index label color (default: #111111).

Implies --saccade-color-by-type, unless --saccade-color-by-direction is given — then it recolors that two-way split (its forward and regression colors). --saccade-classes CLASSES — Draw only these reading classes, comma-separated, e.g. --saccade-classes regression,return_sweep (classes: forward, skip, refixation, return_sweep, regression, other). Pass --highlight-column '' to highlight nothing. How it is drawn is --critical-span-style. --critical-span-style mark-text, mark-border, none — How the --highlight-column words are marked: mark-text recolors them, mark-border outlines their boxes, none draws neither (default: mark-text). --stimulus-image PATH — Draw an image (PNG/JPG) as the stimulus background under the scanpath. Use with --stimulus-image. --stimulus-image-origin X,Y — Top-left of the stimulus image in monitor px, e.g. 305,44 (default: 0,0). Use with --stimulus-image to align a centered crop to the fixation coordinates. --stimulus-image-opacity O — Stimulus-image opacity 0.1–1.0 (default: 1.0 = opaque). Lower it to dim a busy image so the fixations / saccades / word boxes read over it. --show-stimulus-image switch — Draw each trial's own stimulus page under the scanpath: the image_path its rows carry (from --image-root, or a dataset that ships its pages, like --sample), placed at its image_x / image_y. --stimulus-image PATH wins. --text-color COLOR — Reading-text color (default: #000000). --highlight-text-color COLOR — Color of the --highlight-column words under --critical-span-style mark-text (default: #D55E00). --span-border-color COLOR — Box color under --critical-span-style mark-border (default: #000000). --line-spacing N — How far apart the lines are, in font sizes: the reading text is the distance between lines ÷ N (default: 3, a blank line above and below). --no-scale-text-to-boxes switch — Draw the reading text at --font-size instead of sizing it from the word boxes. --font-size PX 16 Base figure font size (default: 16). --font-family NAME — Font for all figure text (default: monospace).

docs.text: Option Value Default Description --word-boxes switch — Draw the word boxes. --no-word-boxes--no-words switch — Hide the word boxes (the default). --word-box-color COLOR — Word-box outline color (default: #6c757d). A comparison outlines each scanpath's boxes in its own color instead. --word-box-line-opacity O — Word-box outline opacity, 0–1; 0 draws the fill only (default: 1). Below 1 the outline color must be #rrggbb, #rgb or rgb(r, g, b). --word-box-fill-color COLOR — Word-box fill color, drawn at --word-box-fill-opacity: #rrggbb, #rgb or rgb(r, g, b) (default: #646464). --word-box-fill-opacity O — Word-box fill opacity, 0–1; 0 draws outlines only (default: 0.05).

docs.title: Heatmap
docs.text: Option Value Default Description --heatmap switch — Draw the heatmap. --no-heatmap switch — Hide the heatmap (the default). --heatmap-metric COLUMN — Heatmap weighting: the fixation duration column — under your file's name or as duration_ms (the default) — or counts. --heatmap-style word-boxes, interpolated — Heatmap geometry (default: word-boxes). --heatmap-sigma PX — Gaussian σ in px for --heatmap-style interpolated (default: 2% of the data's larger span, at least 8 px). --heatmap-colorscale NAME — Heatmap color scale, e.g. Greens (default: Blues). --heatmap-norm linear, log — Heatmap color scaling: linear (default) or log — log compresses heavy-tailed dwell times so a few hot words don't wash out the rest. --heatmap-opacity O — Heatmap opacity, 0.05–1.0 (default: each style's own — word boxes 0.5, or 0.35 with no word boxes; interpolated 0.45). --heatmap-range LO HI — Pin the heatmap's color scale to LO..HI instead of the trial's own range. --word-heatmap-col COLUMN — For a words-only dataset (no fixations): tint each word box by this numeric words column — e.g. gpt2_surprisal — instead of its dwell time. --word-heatmap-title TEXT — Color-bar title for --word-heatmap-col (default: Value).

docs.title: Raw gaze
docs.text: Option Value Default Description --raw-gaze PATH [PATH ...] — Raw (sample-level) gaze table(s) to draw under the fixations, columns auto-detected like --fixations (same formats; several paths or a quoted glob concatenate). Static figures and --compare-with comparisons, where each scanpath's samples take its color (not --animate). On its own (no other input) it is the dataset: its trials are listed and drawn as recorded — no fixations are detected from the samples. --no-raw-gaze switch — Load the --raw-gaze table but hide its layer — the app's 🔵 Raw gaze switch turned off. Shows by default. --no-saccade-type-legend switch — With --saccade-color-by-type: hide the saccade-type color key on the figure (the colored lines still draw). SPEC is KIND=POSITION[,ARRANGEMENT][,SIZE] with KIND one of compare, saccades, colors (the fixation colour categories), size-key, highlight (the highlighted-words note); POSITION auto or SPOT-outside / SPOT-inside with SPOT one of top-left, top-center, top-right, left, right, bottom-left, bottom-center, bottom-right (outside grows the figure; left and right run down the side); ARRANGEMENT stacked or side-by-side; SIZE the text size in px — e.g. --legend saccades=right-outside,stacked,14. docs.title: Comparison

Taken from the loaded dataset unless --compare-words/--compare-fixations name a second one. --compare-screen SCREEN_ID — Screen of the second scanpath's multipart trial (default: its first screen), looked up in its own trial. --screen picks the first scanpath's. Each scanpath is drawn from one screen. --compare-layout overlay, side-by-side, stacked overlay How the two scanpaths are arranged (default: overlay). Across two datasets, overlay needs both canvases to be the same size — two different canvases are refused rather than silently split, so pass side-by-side or stacked for them. Matching canvases that a dataset never recorded still overlay, with a warning. --compare-stimulus both, a, b both On an overlay, whose word boxes and text to draw (default: both). Two datasets' word boxes coincide only when the text is identical. --label-a TEXT — Name for the FIRST scanpath in the legend and hover, instead of the default. Applies to the comparison figure and the --animate co-animation. Requires --label-b. --label-b TEXT — Name for the SECOND scanpath in the legend and hover, instead of the default. Requires --label-a. --compare-legend--no-compare-legend switch — Draw the legend naming the two scanpaths (the app's A/B legend; on by default, as in the app). Applies to the --animate co-animation too. --style-a SPEC — Styling for the FIRST scanpath, repeatable: KEY=VALUE[,...]. Colors (#RRGGBB): fix_color, saccade_color, box_color (word-box outline; default fix_color), box_fill_color (default --word-box-fill-color), raw_gaze_color (default fix_color). Also heatmap_colorscale (default --heatmap-colorscale, on the shared range), saccade_style (solid|dash|dot|dashdot), saccade_width (px), marker_size_range (MIN:MAX), opacity (0.1–1), box_line_opacity / box_fill_opacity (0–1; default --word-box-line-opacity / --word-box-fill-opacity), hollow (true|false). E.g. --style-a fix_color=#D55E00,opacity=0.5. --animate uses them too, except box_color, box_fill_color, the box opacities and raw_gaze_color. --style-b SPEC — Styling for the SECOND scanpath, repeatable: KEY=VALUE[,...]. Colors (#RRGGBB): fix_color, saccade_color, box_color (word-box outline; default fix_color), box_fill_color (default --word-box-fill-color), raw_gaze_color (default fix_color). Also heatmap_colorscale (default --heatmap-colorscale, on the shared range), saccade_style (solid|dash|dot|dashdot), saccade_width (px), marker_size_range (MIN:MAX), opacity (0.1–1), box_line_opacity / box_fill_opacity (0–1; default --word-box-line-opacity / --word-box-fill-opacity), hollow (true|false). E.g. --style-b fix_color=#D55E00,opacity=0.5. --animate uses them too, except box_color, box_fill_color, the box opacities and raw_gaze_color. --compare-fixation-flag SPEC — Filters & highlights for the SECOND scanpath only, repeatable; same SPEC as --fixation-flag, e.g. --compare-fixation-flag short=discard,threshold_ms=80. Replaces --fixation-flag for B. --compare-saccade-classes CLASSES — The reading classes the SECOND scanpath draws, comma-separated (same names as --saccade-classes). Replaces --saccade-classes for B. Not with --animate, which draws every class. --compare-fix-index-range START:END — Draw only fixations START through END of the SECOND scanpath (1-based, inclusive). Replaces --fix-index-range for B. --stimulus-image-b PATH — The SECOND scanpath's stimulus image, for a side-by-side or stacked comparison across two datasets (each panel draws its own page). Same formats and globbing as --words. --compare-fixations PATH [PATH ...] — Fixations table(s) for the SECOND dataset. Same formats and globbing as --fixations. --compare-raw-gaze PATH [PATH ...] — Raw gaze table(s) for the SECOND dataset, drawn under B's scanpath.
